entries.ff5d50e08205792400cd5f8503ebe20fb709a4a0: <div sID="gen5145" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Ruth.2" sID="Ruth.2"/> <div eID="gen5145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5146" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5147" type="x-p"/> There is scarcely any chapter in all the sacred history that stoops so low as this to take cognizance of so mean a person as Ruth, a poor Moabitish widow, so mean an action as her gleaning corn in a neighbour's field, and the minute circumstances thereof. But all this was in order to her being grafted into the line of Christ and taken in among his ancestors, that she might be a figure of the espousals of the Gentile church to Christ, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">Isa. liv. 1</reference>. This makes the story remarkable; and many of the passages of it are instructive and very improvable. Here we have, I. Ruth's humility and industry in gleaming corn, Providence directing her to Boaz's field, <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.1-Ruth.2.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. The great favour which Boaz showed to her in many instances, <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.4-Ruth.2.16">ver. 4-16</reference>. III. The return of Ruth to her mother-in-law, <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.18-Ruth.2.23">ver. 18-23</reference>.
entries.23c1d94ec77a8650177bc02cf0afa9f1e8ac6d38: <div eID="gen5147" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5146" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Ruth in the Field of Boaz. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1312.)</title> <div sID="gen5148" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And Naomi had a kinsman of her husband's, a mighty man of wealth, of the family of Elimelech; and his name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Boaz. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Ruth the Moabitess said unto Naomi, Let me now go to the field, and glean ears of corn after <hi type="italic">him</hi> in whose sight I shall find grace. And she said unto her, Go, my daughter. <hi type="super">3</hi> And she went, and came, and gleaned in the field after the reapers: and her hap was to light on a part of the field <hi type="italic">belonging</hi> unto Boaz, who <hi type="italic">was</hi> of the kindred of Elimelech. <div eID="gen5148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5149" type="x-p"/> Naomi had now gained a settlement in Bethlehem among her old friends; and here we have an account, <div eID="gen5149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5150" type="x-p"/> I. Of her rich kinsman, Boaz, <hi type="italic">a mighty man of wealth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.1">v. 1</reference>. The Chaldee reads it, <hi type="italic">mighty in the law.</hi> If he was both, it was a most rare and excellent conjunction, to be mighty in wealth and mighty in the scriptures too; those that are so are mighty indeed. He was grandson of Nahshon, who was prince of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness, and son of Salmon, probably a younger son, by Rahab, the harlot of Jericho. He carries might in his name, <hi type="italic">Boaz—in him is strength;</hi> and he was of the family of Elimelech, that family which was now reduced and brought so low. Observe, 1. Boaz, though a rich and great man, had poor relations. Every branch of the tree is not a top-branch. Let not those that are great in the world be ashamed to own their kindred that are mean and despised, lest they be found therein proud, scornful, and unnatural. 2. Naomi, though a poor contemptible widow, had rich relations, whom yet she boasted not of, nor was burdensome to, nor expected any thing from when she returned to Bethlehem in distress. Those that have rich relations, while they themselves are poor, ought to know that it is the wise providence of God that makes the difference (in which we ought to acquiesce), and that to be proud of our relation to such is a great sin, and to trust to it is great folly. <div eID="gen5150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5151" type="x-p"/> II. Of her poor daughter-in-law, <reference osisRef="Ruth.1">Ruth. 1</reference>. Her condition was very low and poor, which was a great trial to the faith and constancy of a young proselyte. The Bethlehemites would have done well if they had invited Naomi and her daughter-in-law first to one good house and then to another (it would have been a great support to an aged widow and a great encouragement to a new convert); but, instead of tasting the dainties of Canaan, they have no way of getting necessary food but by gleaning corn, and otherwise, for aught that appears, they might have starved. Note, <hi type="italic">God has chosen the poor of this world;</hi> and poor they are likely to be, for, though God has chosen them, commonly men overlook them. 2. Her character, in this condition, was very good <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.2">(v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">She said to Naomi,</hi> not, "Let me now go to the land of Moab again, for there is no living here, here there is want, but <hi type="italic">in my father's house there is bread enough.</hi>" No, she is <hi type="italic">not mindful of the country from which she came out,</hi> otherwise she had now a fair occasion to return. The God of Israel shall be her God, and, though he slay her, yet will she trust in him and never forsake him. But her request is, <hi type="italic">Let me go to the field, and glean ears of corn.</hi> Those that are well born, and have been well brought up, know not what straits they may be reduced to, nor what mean employments they may be obliged to get their bread by, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.5">Lam. iv. 5</reference>. When the case is thus melancholy, let Ruth be remembered, who is a great example, (1.) Of humility. When Providence had made her poor she did not say, "To glean, which is in effect to beg, I am ashamed," but cheerfully stoops to the meanness of her circumstances and accommodates herself to her lot. High spirits can more easily starve than stoop; Ruth was none of those. She does not tell her mother she was never brought up to live upon crumbs. Though she was not brought up to it, she is brought down to it, and is not uneasy at it. Nay, it is her own motion, not her mother's injunction. Humility is one of the brightest ornaments of youth, and one of the best omens. Before Ruth's honour was this humility. Observe how humbly she speaks of herself, in her expectation of leave to glean: Let me glean after him <hi type="italic">in whose sight I shall find grace.</hi> She does not say, "I will go and glean, and surely nobody will deny me the liberty," but, "I will go and glean, in the hope that somebody will allow me the liberty." Note, Poor people must not demand kindness as a debt, but humbly ask it, and take it as a favour, though in ever so small a matter. It becomes the poor to use entreaties. (2.) Of industry. She does not say to her mother-in-law, "Let me now go a visiting to the ladies of the town, or go a walking in the fields to take the air and be merry; I cannot sit all day moping with you." No, it is not sport, but business, that her heart is upon: "<hi type="italic">Let me go and glean ears of corn,</hi> which will turn to some good account." She was one of those virtuous women that love not to eat the bread of idleness, but love to take pains. This is an example to young people. Let them learn betimes to labour, and, <hi type="italic">what their hand finds to do, do it with their might.</hi> A disposition to diligence bodes well both for this world and the other. Love not sleep, love not sport, love not sauntering; but love business. It is also an example to poor people to work for their living, and not beg that which they are able to earn. We must not be shy of any honest employment, though it be mean, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ergon ouden oneidos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">No labour is a reproach.</hi> Sin is a thing below us, but we must not think any thing else so that Providence calls us to. (3.) Of regard to her mother. Though she was but her mother-in-law, and though, being loosed by death from the law of her husband, she might easily suppose herself thereby loosed from the law of her husband's mother, yet she is dutifully observant of her. She will not go out without letting her know and asking her leave. This respect young people ought to show to their parents and governors; it is part of the honour due to them. She did not say, "Mother, if you will go with me, I will go glean:" but, "Do you sit at home and take your ease, and I will go abroad, and take pains." <hi type="italic">Juniores ad labores—Youth should work.</hi> Let young people take advice from the aged, but not put them upon toil. (4.) Of dependence upon Providence, intimated in that, I will <hi type="italic">glean after him in whose sight I shall find grace.</hi> She knows not which way to go, nor whom to enquire for, but will trust Providence to raise her up some friend or other that will be kind to her. Let us always keep us good thoughts of the divine providence, and believe that while we do well it will do well for us. And it did well for Ruth; for when she went out alone, without guide or companion, to glean, <hi type="italic">her hap was to light on the field of Boaz,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.3">v. 3</reference>. To her it seemed casual. She knew not whose field it was, nor had she any reason for going to that more than any other, and therefore it is said to be <hi type="italic">her hap;</hi> but Providence directed her steps to this field. Note, God wisely orders small events; and those that seem altogether contingent serve his own glory and the good of his people. Many a great affair is brought about by a little turn, which seemed fortuitous to us, but was directed by Providence with design.
entries.863b7f7686e51e43a7d53788862b6b856999b1eb: <div eID="gen5151" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Kindness of Boaz to Ruth. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1312.)</title> <div sID="gen5152" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> And, behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem, and said unto the reapers, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">be</hi> with you. And they answered him, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> bless thee. <hi type="super">5</hi> Then said Boaz unto his servant that was set over the reapers, Whose damsel <hi type="italic">is</hi> this? <hi type="super">6</hi> And the servant that was set over the reapers answered and said, It <hi type="italic">is</hi> the Moabitish damsel that came back with Naomi out of the country of Moab: <hi type="super">7</hi> And she said, I pray you, let me glean and gather after the reapers among the sheaves: so she came, and hath continued even from the morning until now, that she tarried a little in the house. <hi type="super">8</hi> Then said Boaz unto Ruth, Hearest thou not, my daughter? Go not to glean in another field, neither go from hence, but abide here fast by my maidens: <hi type="super">9</hi> <hi type="italic">Let</hi> thine eyes <hi type="italic">be</hi> on the field that they do reap, and go thou after them: have I not charged the young men that they shall not touch thee? and when thou art athirst, go unto the vessels, and drink of <hi type="italic">that</hi> which the young men have drawn. <hi type="super">10</hi> Then she fell on her face, and bowed herself to the ground, and said unto him, Why have I found grace in thine eyes, that thou shouldest take knowledge of me, seeing I <hi type="italic">am</hi> a stranger? <hi type="super">11</hi> And Boaz answered and said unto her, It hath fully been showed me, all that thou hast done unto thy mother in law since the death of thine husband: and <hi type="italic">how</hi> thou hast left thy father and thy mother, and the land of thy nativity, and art come unto a people which thou knewest not heretofore. <hi type="super">12</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust. <hi type="super">13</hi> Then she said, Let me find favour in thy sight, my lord; for that thou hast comforted me, and for that thou hast spoken friendly unto thine handmaid, though I be not like unto one of thine handmaidens. <hi type="super">14</hi> And Boaz said unto her, At mealtime come thou hither, and eat of the bread, and dip thy morsel in the vinegar. And she sat beside the reapers: and he reached her parched <hi type="italic">corn,</hi> and she did eat, and was sufficed, and left. <hi type="super">15</hi> And when she was risen up to glean, Boaz commanded his young men, saying, Let her glean even among the sheaves, and reproach her not: <hi type="super">16</hi> And let fall also <hi type="italic">some</hi> of the handfuls of purpose for her, and leave <hi type="italic">them,</hi> that she may glean <hi type="italic">them</hi>, and rebuke her not. <div eID="gen5152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5153" type="x-p"/> Now Boaz himself appears, and a great deal of decency there appears in his carriage both towards his own servants and towards this poor stranger. <div eID="gen5153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5154" type="x-p"/> I. Towards his own servants, and those that were employed for him in reaping and gathering in his corn. Harvest-time is busy time, many hands must then be at work. Boaz that had much, being a mighty man of wealth, had much to do, and consequently many to work under him and to live upon him. <hi type="italic">As goods are increased those are increased that eat them, and what good has the owner thereof save the beholding of them with his eyes?</hi> Boaz is here an example of a good master. <div eID="gen5154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5155" type="x-p"/> 1. He had a servant that was set over the reapers, <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.6">v. 6</reference>. In great families it is requisite there should be one to oversee the rest of the servants, and appoint to each their portion both of work and meat. Ministers are such servants in God's house, and it is requisite that they be both wise and faithful, and <hi type="italic">show their Lord all things,</hi> as he here, <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.6">v. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen5155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5156" type="x-p"/> 2. Yet he came himself to his reapers, to see how the work went forward, if he found any thing amiss to rectify it, and to give further orders what should be done. This was both for his own interest (he that wholly leaves his business to others will have it done by the halves; the master's eye makes a fat horse) and it was also for the encouragement of his servants, who would go on the more cheerfully in their work when their master countenanced them so far as to make them a visit. Masters that live at ease should think with tenderness of those that toil for them and bear the burden and heat of the day. <div eID="gen5156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5157" type="x-p"/> 3. Kind and pious salutations were interchanged between Boaz and his reapers. <div eID="gen5157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5158" type="x-p"/> (1.) He said to them, <hi type="italic">The Lord be with you;</hi> and they replied, <hi type="italic">The Lord bless thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.4">v. 4</reference>. Hereby they expressed, [1.] Their mutual respect to each other; he to them as good servants, and they to him as a good master. When he came to them he did not fall a chiding them, as if he came only to find fault and exercise his authority, but he prayed for them: "<hi type="italic">The Lord be with you,</hi> prosper you, and give you health and strength, and preserve you from any disaster." Nor did they, as soon as ever he was out of hearing, fall a cursing him, as some ill-natured servants that hate their master's eye, but they returned his courtesy: "<hi type="italic">The Lord bless thee,</hi> and make our labours serviceable to thy prosperity." Things are likely to go on well in a house where there is such good-will as this between master and servants. [2.] Their joint-dependence upon the divine providence. They express their kindness to each other by praying one for another. They show not only their courtesy, but their piety, and acknowledgement that all good comes from the presence and blessing of God, which therefore we should value and desire above any thing else both for ourselves and others. <div eID="gen5158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5159" type="x-p"/> (2.) Let us hence learn to use, [1.] Courteous salutations, as expressions of a sincere good-will to our friends. [2.] Pious ejaculations, lifting up our hearts to God for his favour, in such short prayers as these. Only we must take heed that they do not degenerate into formality, lest in them we <hi type="italic">take the name of the Lord our God in vain;</hi> but, if we be serious in them, we may in them keep up our communion with God, and fetch in mercy and grace from him. It appears to have been the usual custom thus to wish reapers good speed, <reference osisRef="Ps.129.7-Ps.129.8">Ps. cxxix. 7, 8</reference>. <div eID="gen5159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5160" type="x-p"/> 4. He took an account from his reapers concerning a stranger he met with in the field, and gave necessary orders concerning her, that they should not touch her (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.9">v. 9</reference>) nor reproach her, <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.15">v. 15</reference>. Masters must take care, not only that they do no hurt themselves, but that they suffer not their servants and those under them to do hurt. He also ordered them to be kind to her, and <hi type="italic">let fall some of the handfuls on purpose for her.</hi> Though it is fit that masters should restrain and rebuke their servants' wastefulness, yet they should not tie them up from being charitable, but give them allowance for that, with prudent directions. <div eID="gen5160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5161" type="x-p"/> II. Boaz was very kind to Ruth, and showed her a great deal of favour, induced to it by the account he had of her, and what he observed concerning her, God also inclining his heart to countenance her. Coming among his reapers, he observed this stranger among them, and got intelligence from his steward who she was, and here is a very particular account of what passed concerning her. <div eID="gen5161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5162" type="x-p"/> 1. The steward gave to Boaz a very fair account of her, proper to recommend her to his favour, <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.6-Ruth.2.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. (1.) That she was a stranger, and therefore one of those that by the law of God were to <hi type="italic">gather the gleanings of the harvest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.19.9-Lev.19.10">Lev. xix. 9, 10</reference>. She is the Moabitish damsel. (2.) That she was allied to his family; she came back with Naomi, the wife of Elimelech, a kinsman of Boaz. (3.) That she was a proselyte, for she came out of the country of Moab to settle in the land of Israel. (4.) That she was very modest, and had not gleaned till she had asked leave. (5.) That she was very industrious, and had continued close to her work from morning even until now. And the poor that are industrious and willing to take pains are fit to be encouraged. Now, in the heat of the day, she tarried a little in the house or booth that was set up in the field for shelter from the weather to repose herself, and some suggest that it is probably she retired for her devotion. But she soon came back to her work, and, except that little intermission, kept close to it all day, though it was not what she had been used to. Servants should be just in the character and reports they give to their masters, and take heed they do not misrepresent any person, nor without cause discourage their master's charity. <div eID="gen5162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5163" type="x-p"/> 2. Boaz was hereupon extremely civil to her in divers instances. (1.) He ordered her to attend his reapers in every field they gathered in and not to glean in the field of another, for she should not need to go any where else to better herself (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Abide here fast by my maidens;</hi> for those of her own sex were the fittest company for her. (2.) He charged all his servants to be very tender of her and respectful to her, and no doubt they would be so to one to whom they saw their master kind. She was a stranger, and it is probably her language, dress, and mien differed much from theirs; but he charged them that they should not in any thing affront her, or be abusive to her, as rude servants are too apt to be to strangers. (3.) He bade her welcome to the entertainment he had provided for his own servants. He ordered her, not only to drink of the water which was drawn for them (for that seems to be the liquor he means, <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.9">v. 9</reference>, drawn from the famous well of Beth-lehem which was by the gate, the water of which David longed for, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.15">2 Sam. xxiii. 15</reference>), but <hi type="italic">at meal-time to come and eat of their bread</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.14">v. 14</reference>), yea, and she should be welcome to their sauce too: <hi type="italic">Come, dip thy morsel in the vinegar,</hi> to make it savoury; for God allows us not only nourishing but relishing food, not for necessity only, but for delight. And for encouragement to her, and direction to the servants, he himself, happening to be present when the reapers sat down to meat, <hi type="italic">reached her parched corn</hi> to eat. It is no disparagement to the finest hand to be <hi type="italic">reached forth to the needy</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.20">Prov. xxxi. 20</reference>), and to be employed in serving the poor. Observe, Boaz was not scanty in his provision for his reapers, but sent them so much more than enough for themselves as would be entertainment for a stranger. Thus <hi type="italic">there is that scattereth and yet increaseth.</hi> (4.) He commended her for her dutiful respect to her mother-in-law, which, though he did not know her by sight, yet he had heard of (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">It has been fully shown me all that thou hast done unto thy mother-in-law.</hi> Note, Those that do well ought to have the praise of it. But that which especially he commended her for was that she had left her own country, and had become a proselyte to the Jewish religion; for so the Chaldee expounds it: "Thou hast come to be proselyted, and to dwell among <hi type="italic">a people whom thou knowest not.</hi>" Those that leave all, to embrace the true religion, are worthy of double honour. (5.) He prayed for her (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord recompense thy work.</hi> Her strong affection to the commonwealth of Israel, to which she was by birth an alien, was such a work of the divine grace in her as would certainly be crowned with a full reward by him <hi type="italic">under whose wings she had come to trust.</hi> Note, Those that by faith come under the wings of the divine grace, and have a full complacency and confidence in that grace, may be sure of a full recompence of reward for their so doing. From this expression, the Jews describe a proselyte to be one that is <hi type="italic">gathered under the wings of the divine majesty.</hi> (6.) He encouraged her to go on in her gleaning, and did not offer to take her off from that; for the greatest kindness we can do our poor relations is to assist and encourage their industry. Boaz ordered his servants to let her glean among the sheaves, where other gleaners were not allowed to come, and not to reproach her, that is, not to call her <hi type="italic">thief,</hi> or to suspect her of taking more than was allowed her, <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.15">v. 15</reference>. All this shows Boaz to have been a man of a generous spirit, and one that, according to the law, considered the heart of a stranger. <div eID="gen5163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5164" type="x-p"/> 3. Ruth received his favours with a great deal of humility and gratitude, and conducted herself with as much propriety in her place as he did himself in his, but little thinking that she should shortly be the mistress of that field she was now gleaning in. (1.) She paid all possible respect to him, and gave him honour, according to the usage of the country (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">She fell on her face, and bowed herself to the ground.</hi> Note, Good breeding is a great ornament to religion; and we must render <hi type="italic">honour to whom honour is due.</hi> (2.) She humbly owned herself unworthy of his favours: "<hi type="italic">I am a stranger</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.10">v. 10</reference>) and <hi type="italic">not like one of thy handmaids</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.13">v. 13</reference>), not so well dressed nor so well taught, not so neat nor so handy." Note, It well becomes us all to think meanly of ourselves, and to take notice of that in ourselves which is diminishing, esteeming others better than ourselves. (3.) She gratefully acknowledged his kindness to her; though it was no great expense to him, nor much more than what he was obliged to by the divine law, yet she magnifies and admires it: <hi type="italic">Why have I found grace in thy eyes?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.10">v. 10</reference>. (4.) She begs the continuance of his good-will: <hi type="italic">Let me find favour in they sight</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.13">v. 13</reference>), and owns that what he had said had been a cordial to her: <hi type="italic">Thou hast comforted me, for that thou hast spoken friendly to me.</hi> Those that are great, and in high places, know not how much good they may do to their inferiors with a kind look or by speaking friendly to them; and so small an expense, one would think, they should not grudge, when it shall be put upon the score of their charity. (5.) When Boaz gave her her dinner with his reapers she only ate so much as would suffice her, and left the rest, and immediately rose up to glean, <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.14-Ruth.2.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. She did not, under pretence either of her want or of her labour, eat more than was convenient for her, nor so much as to unfit her for work in the afternoon. Temperance is a friend to industry; and we must eat and drink to strengthen us for business, not to indispose us to it.
entries.fcf42bd0092ad6b34290c3c48e4677c0f0b20d5a: <div eID="gen5164" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Ruth's Report to Naomi. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1312.)</title> <div sID="gen5165" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> So she gleaned in the field until even, and beat out that she had gleaned: and it was about an ephah of barley. <hi type="super">18</hi> And she took <hi type="italic">it</hi> up, and went into the city: and her mother in law saw what she had gleaned: and she brought forth, and gave to her that she had reserved after she was sufficed. <hi type="super">19</hi> And her mother in law said unto her, Where hast thou gleaned to day? and where wroughtest thou? blessed be he that did take knowledge of thee. And she showed her mother in law with whom she had wrought, and said, The man's name with whom I wrought to day <hi type="italic">is</hi> Boaz. <hi type="super">20</hi> And Naomi said unto her daughter in law, Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> he of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , who hath not left off his kindness to the living and to the dead. And Naomi said unto her, The man <hi type="italic">is</hi> near of kin unto us, one of our next kinsmen. <hi type="super">21</hi> And Ruth the Moabitess said, He said unto me also, Thou shalt keep fast by my young men, until they have ended all my harvest. <hi type="super">22</hi> And Naomi said unto Ruth her daughter in law, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> good, my daughter, that thou go out with his maidens, that they meet thee not in any other field. <hi type="super">23</hi> So she kept fast by the maidens of Boaz to glean unto the end of barley harvest and of wheat harvest; and dwelt with her mother in law. <div eID="gen5165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5166" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Ruth finishes her day's work, <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.17">v. 17</reference>. 1. She took care not to lose time, for she gleaned until evening. We must not be weary of well-doing, because in due season we shall reap. She did not make an excuse to sit still, or go home, till the evening. Let us <hi type="italic">work the works of him that sent us, while it is day.</hi> She scarcely used, much less did she abuse, the kindness of Boaz; for, though he ordered his servants to leave handfuls for her, she continued to glean the scattered ears. 2. She took care not to lose what she had gathered, but threshed it herself, that she might the more easily carry it home, and might have it ready for use. <hi type="italic">The slothful man roasteth not that which he took in hunting,</hi> and so loseth the benefit of it, <hi type="italic">but the substance of a diligent man is precious,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.27">Prov. xii. 27</reference>. Ruth had gathered it ear by ear, but, when she had put it all together, it was an ephah of barley, about four pecks. Many a little makes a great deal. It is an encouragement to industry that in all labour, even that of gleaning, there is profit, but the <hi type="italic">talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.</hi> When she had got her corn into as little compass as she could, she took it up herself, and carried it into the city, though, had she asked them, it is likely some of Boaz's servants would have done that for her. We should study to be as little as possible troublesome to those that are kind to us. She did not think it either too hard or too mean a service to carry her corn herself into the city, but was rather pleased with what she had gotten by her own industry, and careful to secure it; and let us thus take care that we <hi type="italic">lose not those things which we have wrought,</hi> which we have gained, <reference osisRef="2John.1.8">2 John 8</reference>. <div eID="gen5166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5167" type="x-p"/> II. She paid her respects to her mother-in-law, went straight home to her and did not go to converse with Boaz's servants, <hi type="italic">showed her what she had gleaned,</hi> that she might see she had not been idle. <div eID="gen5167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5168" type="x-p"/> 1. She entertained her with what she had left of the good dinner Boaz had given her. She gave to her what she had reserved, after she was sufficed (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.18">v. 18</reference>), which refers to <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.14">v. 14</reference>. If she had any thing better than another, her mother should have part with her. Thus, having shown industry abroad, she showed piety at home; so children's maintaining their parents is called (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.4">1 Tim. v. 4</reference>), and it is part of the honour due to them by the fifth commandment, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.6">Matt. xv. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen5168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5169" type="x-p"/> 2. She gave her an account of her day's work, and how a kind providence had favoured her in it, which made it very comfortable to her; for the gleanings that a righteous man hath are better than the harvests of many wicked, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.16">Ps. xxxvii. 16</reference>. (1.) Naomi asked her where she had been: <hi type="italic">Where hast thou gleaned to-day?</hi> Note, Parents should take care to enquire into the ways of their children, how, and where, and in what company they spend their time. This may prevent many extravagancies which children, left to themselves, run into, by which they bring both themselves and their parents to shame. If we are not our brethren's, yet surely we are our children's keepers: and we know what a son Adonijah proved, that had never been chidden. Parents should examine their children, not to frighten nor discourage them, not so as to make them hate home or tempt them to tell a lie, but to commend them if they have done well, and with mildness to reprove and caution them if they have done otherwise. It is a good question for us to ask ourselves in the close of every day, "<hi type="italic">Where have I gleaned to-day?</hi> What improvements have I made in knowledge and grace? What have I done or obtained that will turn to a good account?" (2.) Ruth gave her a particular account of the kindness she had received from Boaz (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.19">v. 19</reference>) and the hopes she had of further kindness from him, he having ordered her to attend his servants throughout all the harvest, <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.21">v. 21</reference>. Note, Children should look upon themselves as accountable to their parents and to those that are over them, and not think it a disparagement to them to be examined; let them <hi type="italic">do that which is good,</hi> and they shall have praise of the same. Ruth told her mother what kindness Boaz had shown her, that she might take some occasion or another to acknowledge it and return him thanks; but she did not tell her how Boaz had commended her, <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.11">v. 11</reference>. Humility teaches us, not only not to praise ourselves, but not to be forward to publish others' praises of us. (3.) We are here told what Naomi said to it. [1.] She prayed heartily for him that had been her daughter's benefactor, even before she knew who it was (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Blessed be he,</hi> whoever he was, <hi type="italic">that did take knowledge of thee,</hi> shooting the arrow of prayer at a venture. But more particularly when she was told who it was (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">Blessed be he of the Lord.</hi> Note, The poor must pray for those that are kind and liberal to them, and thus requite them, when they are not capable of making them any other requital. Let the loins of the poor bless those that refresh them, <reference osisRef="Job.29.13">Job xxix. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.20">xxxi. 20</reference>. And he that hears the cries of the poor against their oppressors (<reference osisRef="Exod.22.27">Exod. xxii. 27</reference>), it may be hoped, will hear the prayers of the poor for their benefactors. She now remembered the former kindnesses Boaz had shown to her husband and sons, and joins those to this: he has not <hi type="italic">left off his kindness to the living and to the dead.</hi> If we generously show kindness even to those that seem to have forgotten our former favours, perhaps it may help to revive the remembrance even of those which seem buried. [2.] She acquainted Ruth with the relation their family was in to Boaz: <hi type="italic">The man is near of kin to us.</hi> It should seem she had been so long in Moab that she had forgotten her kindred in the land of Israel, till by this providence God brought it to her mind. At least she had not told Ruth of it, though it might have been some encouragement to a young proselyte. Unlike to humble Naomi are many, who, though fallen into decay themselves, are continually boasting of their great relations. Nay, Observe the chain of thought here, and in it a chain of providences, bringing about what was designed concerning Ruth. Ruth names Boaz as one that had been kind to her. Naomi bethinks herself who that should be, and presently recollects herself: "<hi type="italic">The man is near of kin to us;</hi> now that I hear his name, I remember him very well." This thought brings in another: "He is <hi type="italic">our next kinsman,</hi> our <hi type="italic">goel,</hi> that has the right to redeem our estate that was mortgaged, and therefore from him we may expect further kindness. He is the likeliest man in all Bethlehem to set us up." Thus God brings things to our mind, sometimes on a sudden, that prove to have a wonderful tendency to our good. [3.] She appointed Ruth to continue her attendance in the fields of Boaz (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.22">v. 22</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Let them not meet thee in any other field,</hi> for that will be construed a contempt of his courtesy." Our blessed Saviour is our <hi type="italic">Goel;</hi> it is he that has a right to redeem. If we expect to receive benefit by him, let us closely adhere to him, and his fields, and his family; let us not go to the world and its fields for that which is to be had with him only, and which he has encouraged us to expect from him. Has the Lord dealt bountifully with us? Let us not be found in any other field, nor seek for happiness and satisfaction in the creature. Tradesmen take it ill if those that are in their books go to another shop. We lose divine favours if we slight them. Some think Naomi gave her daughter-in-law a tacit rebuke; she had spoken (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.21">v. 21</reference>) of keeping fast by the young <hi type="italic">men.</hi> "Nay," said Naomi (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.22">v. 22</reference>), "<hi type="italic">It is good that thou go out with his maidens; they</hi> are fitter company for thee than the <hi type="italic">young men.</hi>" But they are too critical. Ruth spoke of the young men because they were the principal labourers, and to them Boaz had given directions concerning her; and Naomi takes it for granted that, while she attended the young men, her society would be with the maidens, as was fit. Ruth dutifully observed her mother's directions; she continued to glean, to the end, not only of barley-harvest, but of the wheat-harvest, which followed it, that she might gather food in harvest to serve for winter, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.6-Prov.6.8">Prov. vi. 6-8</reference>. She also kept fast by the maidens of Boaz, with whom she afterwards cultivated an acquaintance, which might do her service, <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.23">v. 23</reference>. But she constantly came to her mother at night in due time, as became a virtuous woman, that was for working days, and not for merry nights. And when the harvest was ended (as bishop Patrick expounds it) she did not gad abroad, but kept her aged mother company at home. Dinah went out to see the daughters of the land, and we know what a disgrace her vanity ended in. Ruth kept at home, and helped to maintain her mother, and went out on no other errand than to get provision for her, and we shall find afterwards what preferment her humility and industry ended in. <hi type="italic">Seest thou a man diligent in his business?</hi> Honour is before him.  <chapter eID="Ruth.2"/> <div eID="gen5169" type="x-p"/>

entries.08881096092f61eeb605f43dc0a0980ff9346acd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2470"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ruth.2.1-Ruth.2.3">Ru 2:1-3</reference>. Ruth Gleans in the Field of Boaz.</title> <div sID="gen3333" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2470"/><hi type="bold">2. Ruth ... said unto Naomi, Let me now go to the field, and glean--</hi>The right of gleaning was conferred by a positive law on the widow, the poor, and the stranger (see on <reference osisRef="Lev.19.9">Le 19:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.24.19">De 24:19</reference>). But liberty to glean behind the reapers [Ru 2:3] was not a right that could be claimed; it was a privilege granted or refused according to the good will or favor of the owner. <div eID="gen3333" type="x-p"/>
entries.c01bb7e4d6e3e48a4b4f638bbb029e69920e3a93: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2471"/><div sID="gen3334" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2471"/><hi type="bold">3. her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz--</hi>Fields in Palestine being unenclosed, the phrase signifies that portion of the open ground which lay within the landmarks of Boaz. <div eID="gen3334" type="x-p"/>
entries.a4ad9a9c274c233a2d9b7ec52c8f49be1d746c2f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2472"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ruth.2.4-Ruth.2.23">Ru 2:4-23</reference>. He Takes Knowledge of Her, and Shows Her Favor.</title> <div sID="gen3335" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2472"/><hi type="bold">4. Boaz came from Beth-lehem, and said unto the reapers, The Lord be with you--</hi>This pious salutation between the master and his laborers strongly indicates the state of religious feeling among the rural population of Israel at that time, as well as the artless, happy, and unsuspecting simplicity which characterized the manners of the people. The same patriarchal style of speaking is still preserved in the East. <div eID="gen3335" type="x-p"/>
entries.a421e0406e81d1c2e4639b3231f9b4f55a1a6b05: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2473"/><div sID="gen3336" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2473"/><hi type="bold">5. his servant that was set over the reapers--</hi>an overseer whose special duty was to superintend the operations in the field, to supply provision to the reapers, and pay them for their labor in the evening. <div eID="gen3336" type="x-p"/>
entries.9352022f7816a0b03fe8888c3f41d01e4e3e1e17: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2474"/><div sID="gen3337" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2474"/><hi type="bold">7. she said ... Let me glean and gather after the reapers among the sheaves--</hi>Various modes of reaping are practised in the East. Where the crop is thin and short, it is plucked up by the roots. Sometimes it is cut with the sickle. Whether reaped in the one way or the other, the grain is cast into sheaves loosely thrown together, to be subjected to the process of threshing, which takes place, for the most part, immediately after the reaping. Field labors were begun early in the morning--before the day became oppressively hot.<div eID="gen3337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3338" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">she tarried a little in the house--</hi>that is, the field tent, erected for the occasional rest and refreshment of the laborers. <div eID="gen3338" type="x-p"/>
entries.41209e76a98f87862a9bc7d8489dbab59990f968: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2475"/><div sID="gen3339" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2475"/><hi type="bold">8-9. said Boaz unto Ruth, ... bide here fast by my maidens--</hi>The reaping was performed by women while the assortment of sheaves was the duty of men-servants. The same division of harvest labor obtains in Syria still. Boaz not only granted to Ruth the full privilege of gleaning after his reapers, but provided for her personal comfort. <div eID="gen3339" type="x-p"/>
entries.e81099055168a543b023d683c3bf2d1665ef3925: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2477"/><div sID="gen3341" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2477"/><hi type="bold">14. he reached her parched corn, and she did eat, and was sufficed, and left--</hi>some of the new grain, roasted on the spot, and fit for use after being rubbed in the hands--a favorite viand in the East. He gave her so much, that after satisfying her own wants, she had some (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.18">Ru 2:18</reference>) in reserve for her mother-in-law. <div eID="gen3341" type="x-p"/>
entries.93380d5c4226b27d4ce56e63345ebef9b85e739b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2478"/><div sID="gen3342" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2478"/><hi type="bold">16. let fall also some of the handfuls of purpose for her--</hi>The gleaners in the East glean with much success; for a great quantity of corn is scattered in the reaping, as well as in their manner of carrying it. One may judge, then, of the large quantity which Ruth would gather in consequence of the liberal orders given to the servants. These extraordinary marks of favor were not only given from a kindly disposition, but from regard to her good character and devoted attachment to her venerable relative. <div eID="gen3342" type="x-p"/>
entries.f77b812eb7dbba583c716188ae57e65929920441: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2479"/><div sID="gen3343" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2479"/><hi type="bold">17. and beat out that she had gleaned--</hi>When the quantity of grain was small, it was beat out by means of a stick.<div eID="gen3343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3344" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">an ephah--</hi>supposed to contain about a bushel. <div eID="gen3344" type="x-p"/>
entries.189d07e31194f1f677aefe7cd16364b1dbea11e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2480"/><div sID="gen3345" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2480"/><hi type="bold">20. the man is ... one of our next kinsmen--</hi>Hebrew, "one of our redeemers," on whom it devolves to protect us, to purchase our lands, and marry you, the widow of his next kinsman. She said, "one of them," not that there were many in the same close relationship, but that he was a very near kinsman, one other individual only having the precedence. <div eID="gen3345" type="x-p"/>
entries.75c50c4d6d557be20406ce827b848aa2e874265d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2481"/><div sID="gen3346" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2481"/><hi type="bold">21. all my harvest--</hi>both barley and wheat harvests. The latter was at the end of May or the beginning of June. <div eID="gen3346" type="x-p"/>
entries.cba3cc8b0f648a6aefefe4a38bb6b097d6e3d035: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2482"/><div sID="gen3347" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2482"/><hi type="bold">22. Naomi said unto Ruth ... It is good ... that thou go out with his maidens--</hi>a prudent recommendation to Ruth to accept the generous invitation of Boaz, lest, if she were seen straying into other fields, she might not only run the risk of rude treatment, but displease him by seeming indifferent to his kind liberality. Moreover, the observant mind of the old matron had already discerned, in all Boaz' attentions to Ruth, the germs of a stronger affection, which she wished to increase. <chapter eID="Ruth.2"/>

entries.ac274f849202a08fe0845e1c77bec5cf92080f75: <div eID="gen9308" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen9309" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9310" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9310" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9309" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9311" type="x-p"/> Ruth goes to glean in the field of Boaz, <reference osisRef="Rut.2.1-Rut.2.3">Rut 2:1-3</reference>. Boaz finds her, and inquires who she is, <reference osisRef="Rut.2.4-Rut.2.7">Rut 2:4-7</reference>. He speaks kindly to her, gives her permission to follow his reapers, and orders them to use her well, <reference osisRef="Rut.2.8-Rut.2.16">Rut 2:8-16</reference>. She returns in the evening to Naomi, and tells her of her fare; from whom she receives encouragement and advice, <reference osisRef="Rut.2.17-Rut.2.23">Rut 2:17-23</reference>. <div eID="gen9311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9312" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen9312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9313" type="x-p"/> A mighty man of wealth - We have already seen that some suppose Boaz to have been one of the judges of Israel; he was no doubt a man of considerable property.
entries.58123938b92e7114dbfdabcb3b35fdece18f2f8d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen9313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9314" type="x-p"/> Glean ears of corn - The word glean comes from the French glaner, to gather ears or grains of corn. This was formerly a general custom in England and Ireland; the poor went into the fields and collected the straggling ears of corn after the reapers; and it was long supposed that this was their right, and that the law recognized it. But although it has been an old custom, I find that it is now settled, by a solemn judgment in the court of common pleas, that a right to glean in the harvest field cannot be claimed by any person at common law; see Law Dictionary, article gleaning. Any person may permit or prevent it in his own grounds. By the Irish acts, 25 Hen. VIII., c. 1, and 28 Hen. VIII., c. 24, gleaning and leasing are so restricted as to be in fact prohibited in that part of the United Kingdom. See the note on <reference osisRef="Lev.19.9">Lev 19:9</reference>. <div eID="gen9314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9315" type="x-p"/> After him in whose sight I shall find grace - She did not mean Boaz; but she purposed to go out where they were now reaping, and glean after any person who might permit her, or use her in a friendly manner. The words seem to intimate that, notwithstanding the law of Moses, the gleaners might be prevented by the owner of the field.
entries.391658c35e5cdfb45b81076d02bde7550f332460: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen9315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9316" type="x-p"/> And her hap was - So she was accidentally or providentially led to that part of the cultivated country which belonged to Boaz.
entries.ac31516950e6c82ce1fdbbf2ecac3f38eaf72d79: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen9316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9317" type="x-p"/> Boaz came from Beth-lehem - This salutation between Boaz and his reapers is worthy of particular regard; he said, יהוה עמחם Yehovah immachem, "Jehovah be with you!" They said, יברכך יהוה yebarechecha Yehovah, "May Jehovah bless thee!" Can a pious mind read these godly salutations without wishing for a return of those simple primitive times? The words may be thus paraphrased: "May God be with you, to preserve you from accidents, and strengthen you to accomplish your work!" "May God bless Thee with the increase of the field, and grace to use his bounty to the glory of the Giver!"
entries.efef927ddc65bdb1b496c910f5061ea1eb0ececf: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen9317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9318" type="x-p"/> His servant that was set over the reapers - This was a kind of steward or hind who had the under management of the estate. Some think that an officer of this kind is intended in the description given by Homer of the labors of a harvest field, as represented by Vulcan on one compartment of the shield which he made for Achilles: - Εν δ' ετιθει τεμενος βαθυληΐον· ενθα δ εριθοι Ἡμων, οξειας δρεπανας εν χερσιν εχοντες· Δραγματα δ' αλλα μετ' ογμον επμον επητριμα πιπτον εραζε, Αλλα δ' αμαλλοδετηρες εν ελλεδανοισι δεοντο. Τρεις δ' αρ' αμαλλοδετηρες εφεστασαν· αυταρ οπισθε Παιδες δραγμευοντες, εν αγκαλιδεσσι φεροντες, Ασπερχες παρεχον· βασιλευς δ' εν τοισι σιωπῃ Σκηπτρον εχων ἑστηκει επ' ογμου γηθοσυνος κηρ. Κηρυκες δ' απανευθεν ὑπο δρυΐ δαιτα πενοντο· Βουν δ' ἱερευσαντες μεγαν, αμφεπον· αἱ δε γυναικες Δειπνον εριθοισιν, λευκ' αλφιτα πολλα παλυνον. <div eID="gen9318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9319" type="x-p"/> Iliad xviii., v. 550. <div eID="gen9319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9320" type="x-p"/> There too he form'd the likeness of a field <div eID="gen9320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9321" type="x-p"/> Crowded with corn, in which the reapers toil'd, <div eID="gen9321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9322" type="x-p"/> Each with a sharp-tooth'd sickle in his hand. <div eID="gen9322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9323" type="x-p"/> Along the furrow here, the harvest fell <div eID="gen9323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9324" type="x-p"/> In frequent handfuls; there, they bound the sheaves. <div eID="gen9324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9325" type="x-p"/> Three binders of the sheaves their sultry task <div eID="gen9325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9326" type="x-p"/> All plied industrious, and behind them boys <div eID="gen9326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9327" type="x-p"/> Attended, filling with the corn their arms, <div eID="gen9327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9328" type="x-p"/> And offering still their bundles to be bound. <div eID="gen9328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9329" type="x-p"/> Amid them, staff in hand, the master stood, <div eID="gen9329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9330" type="x-p"/> Enjoying, mute the order of the field: <div eID="gen9330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9331" type="x-p"/> While, shaded by an oak, apart his train <div eID="gen9331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9332" type="x-p"/> Prepared the banquet - a well thriven ox <div eID="gen9332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9333" type="x-p"/> New slain, and the attendant maidens mix'd <div eID="gen9333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9334" type="x-p"/> Large supper for the hinds, of whitest flour. <div eID="gen9334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9335" type="x-p"/> Cowper. <div eID="gen9335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9336" type="x-p"/> This scene is well described; and the person who acts as overseer is here called βασιλευς, king, and his staff is called σκηπτρον, a scepter; and he stands in mute dignity, merely to see that the work is well done, and that each person performs his task; and there appear to me to be gleaners in the description, viz., the boys who gather the handfuls after the three binders. See the Greek.
entries.bfb5dc5a4436b1e31df8a1e93ebae5c5c6c4ab33: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen9336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9337" type="x-p"/> That she tarried a little in the house - It seems as if the reapers were now resting in their tent, and that Ruth had just gone in with them to take her rest also.
entries.8dfb35bf4d98c79a739a385d3c6371d802babe09: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen9337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9338" type="x-p"/> Abide here fast by my maidens - These were probably employed in making bands, and laying on them enough to form a sheaf, which the binders would tie and form into shocks or thraves. When the maidens had gathered up the scattered handfuls thrown down by the reapers, Ruth picked up any straggling heads or ears which they had left.
entries.7de1b71b15019cbd9bd7cd610d433f37876ebba8: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen9338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9339" type="x-p"/> The young men that they shall not touch thee - This was peculiarly necessary, as she was a stranger and unprotected.
entries.5c4bf8d7101f3c5ae0db447bc827982021059371: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen9339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9340" type="x-p"/> Then she fell on her face - Prostrated herself, as was the custom in the East when inferiors approached those of superior rank. The Targum adds to the conversation between Ruth and Boaz: "How, says she, have I obtained grace in thy sight, that thou shouldest acknowledge me who am a stranger and one of the daughters of Moab, of whom it is said, The unclean shall not enter into the congregation of the Lord? And Boaz, answered, It has been certainly told me by the word of the wise, that what the Lord hath decreed, he hath not decreed concerning the women but the men. And it hath been surely said to me by prophecy, that kings and prophets shall proceed from thee because of the good which thou hast done," etc.
entries.818e849d40e8c14aaaa594f821c62d3d3c74fe14: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen9340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9341" type="x-p"/> The Lord recompense thy work - The dutiful respect which thou hast paid to thy husband, and thy tender and affectionate attachment to thy aged mother-in-law. <div eID="gen9341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9342" type="x-p"/> And a full reward be given thee - This is spoken with great modesty and piety: The kindness I show thee is little in comparison of thy desert; God alone can give thee a full reward for thy kindness to thy husband and mother-in-law, and he will do it, because thou art come to trust under his wings - to become a proselyte to his religion. The metaphor is taken from the young of fowls, who, seeing a bird of prey, run to their mother to be covered by her wings from danger, and also to take shelter from storms, tempests, cold, etc. It is evident from this that Ruth had already attached herself to the Jewish religion.
entries.02013af12e8532f83ba7b137f6779aaeca3c6532: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen9342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9343" type="x-p"/> Not like unto one of thine hand-maidens - I am as unworthy of thy regards as any of thine own maidservants, and yet thou showest me distinguished kindness.
entries.95c84ec27019a2e629e5d646c9adcbba055c258b: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen9343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9344" type="x-p"/> Dip thy morsel in the vinegar - The חמץ chomets, which we here translate vinegar, seems to have been some refreshing kind of acid sauce used by the reapers to dip their bread in, which both cooled and refreshed them. Vinegar, rob of fruits, etc., are used for this purpose in the East to the present day; and the custom of the Arabs, according to Dr. Shaw, is to dip the bread and hand together into these cooling and refreshing articles. <div eID="gen9344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9345" type="x-p"/> Parched corn - This was a frequent repast among the ancients in almost all countries; see the notes on <reference osisRef="Lev.2.1-Lev.2.14">Lev 2:1-14</reference> (note).
entries.8b9aa042a5681f75205f819c167af69ee0eeb213: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen9345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9346" type="x-p"/> Let her glean even among the sheaves - This was a privilege; for no person should glean till the sheaves were all bound, and the shocks set up.
entries.5984621888bef41e4e8259681a6ed13e8a07e4d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen9346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9347" type="x-p"/> An ephah of barley - Not less than seven gallons and a half; a good day's work. On Hebrew measures of capacity, see the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.16.16">Exo 16:16</reference>.
entries.c98eba7eceba7e84bf0b1da862e6a232b4a325d5: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen9347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9348" type="x-p"/> And gave to her that she had reserved - As Ruth had received a distinct portion at dinner-time, of which she had more than she could eat, <reference osisRef="Rut.2.14">Rut 2:14</reference>; it appears she brought the rest home to her mother-in-law, as is here related.
entries.a8a8dee670f3a264468e0667f1fb999b9c54e12f: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen9348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9349" type="x-p"/> To the living and to the dead - Naomi and Ruth were the living; and they were also the representatives of Elimelech and Mahlon, who were dead. Naomi was of the family; and Ruth, though not of the family, was a representative of one of its deceased branches, being the widow of Mahlon. <div eID="gen9349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9350" type="x-p"/> One of our next kinsmen - מגאלינו miggoaleynu, of our redeemers, one who has the right to redeem the forfeited inheritance of the family. The word גאל goel signifies a near kinsman - one who by the Mosaic law had a right to redeem an inheritance, and also was permitted to vindicate or revenge the death of his relation by killing the slayer, if he found him out of the cities of refuge. <div eID="gen9350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9351" type="x-p"/> In order to prevent families from running to decay, if a brother died childless, the next unmarried brother took his widow; and the children from that marriage were reputed the children of the deceased brother. The office of the next akin was threefold: <div eID="gen9351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9352" type="x-p"/> 1. It belonged to him to buy back the forfeited inheritance, or the liberty of him who had been obliged to sell himself for a servant. <div eID="gen9352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9353" type="x-p"/> 2. It was his right to avenge the blood of any of the family who had been killed, by killing the murderer. <div eID="gen9353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9354" type="x-p"/> 3. It belonged to him to take the widow of a deceased brother or relative, if he died childless. <div eID="gen9354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9355" type="x-p"/> If the nearest akin in any case refused, he was treated with indignity, lost his right to the inheritance, and the next akin to him might come forward and take the widow, etc., as in the case of Boaz. See <reference osisRef="Rut.4.4-Rut.4.10">Rut 4:4-10</reference>.
entries.907435045cc53e447f63c6f142d5c1bad4be5770: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen9355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9356" type="x-p"/> Keep fast by my young men - The word הנערים hannearim should be translated servants, both the male and female being included in it; the latter especially, as we see in <reference osisRef="Rut.2.22">Rut 2:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rut.2.23">Rut 2:23</reference>.
entries.80a5946c0b07bb913dffa63dab5131c7fbc8bdb1: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen9356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9357" type="x-p"/> And of wheat harvest - That is, she was to continue gleaning in the farm of Boaz to the end of the barley harvest; and then, when the wheat harvest began, to continue to its conclusion in the same way. In the interim, as well as each night, she lodged with her mother-in-law. <div eID="gen9357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9358" type="x-p"/> 1. Ruth seems to have been a woman of a very amiable mind: she was modest, and she was industrious, and most probably a comely woman; and all these things served to attract the attention of Boaz, and to engage his affection. Her attachment also to her mother-in-law could not fail to secure his esteem. All these things worked together in the course of Providence, to bring about a matrimonial connection, which in its issue was intimately connected with the salvation of a lost world; for, from this very line, Jesus Christ, according to the flesh, sprang; and Ruth showed herself as worthy to be one of His progenitors as the Virgin Mary was to be His mother. See the notes on Matthew 1:1-16 (note). <div eID="gen9358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9359" type="x-p"/> 2. We should carefully attend to the leadings and to the workings of God's providence; it is our duty and our interest to do both, for the path of duty is ever the way of safety. Had not Ruth acted thus, how dreary and uncomfortable must her life have been! but she followed God fully, and in a path apparently dangerous, and yet, not only sustained no injury, but succeeded well in all things: from this, as well as from innumerable other circumstances, we see the truth of that word, Acknowledge him in all thy ways, and he will direct thy steps; and with this we may ever connect, Trust in the Lord with thy whole heart, and lean not to thy own understanding. Whosoever follows God in simplicity of heart, will most assuredly be guided into all truth.  <chapter eID="Ruth.2"/> <div eID="gen9359" type="x-p"/>

entries.a0d4c45729d4e6f230156b0119d3d82247e07347: s2 Ruth Gleans in the Field of Boaz - Ruth 2 <div eID="gen3566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3567" type="x-p"/> Ruth went to the field to glean ears of corn, for the purpose of procuring support for herself and her mother-in-law, and came by chance to the field of Boaz, a relative of Naomi, who, when he heard that she had come with Naomi from Moabitis, spoke kindly to her, and gave her permission not only to glean ears in his field and even among the sheaves, but to appease her hunger and thirst with the food and drink of his reapers (vv. 1-16), so that in the evening she returned to her mother-in-law with a plentiful gleaning, and told her of the gracious reception she had met with from this man, and then learned from her that Boaz was a relation of her own (Rth 2:17-23). <div eID="gen3567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3568" type="x-p"/> Rth 2:1 <div eID="gen3568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3569" type="x-p"/> The account of this occurrence commences with a statement which was necessary in order to make it perfectly intelligible, namely that Boaz, to whose field Ruth went to glean, was a relative of Naomi through her deceased husband Elimelech. The <hi type="italic">Kethibh</hi> מידע is to be read מידּע, an acquaintance (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.31.12">Psa 31:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.14">Psa 55:14</reference>). The <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> מודע is the construct state of מודע, <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. acquaintanceship, then an acquaintance or friend (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.4">Pro 7:4</reference>), for which מודעת occurs afterwards in Rth 3:2 with the same meaning. That the acquaintance or friend of Naomi through her husband was also a relation, is evident from the fact that he was “of the family of Elimelech. ” According to the rabbinical tradition, which is not well established however, Boaz was a nephew of Elimelech. The ל before אישׁהּ is used instead of the simple construct state, because the reference is not to <hi type="italic">the</hi> relation, but to <hi type="italic">a</hi> relation of her husband; at the same time, the word מודע has taken the form of the construct state notwithstanding this ל (compare <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §292, <hi type="italic">a</hi>., with §289, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.). חיל גּבּור generally means the brave man of war (Jdg 6:12; Jdg 11:1, etc.); but here it signifies a man of property. The name <hi type="italic">Boaz</hi> is not formed from עז בּו, in whom is strength, but from a root, בּעז, which does not occur in Hebrew, and signifies <hi type="italic">alacrity</hi>.
entries.dd279b87c5adb1cc50c3f501fda6c9d418ed5d6e: Rth 2:2-3 <div eID="gen3569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3570" type="x-p"/> Ruth wished to go to the field and glean at (among) the ears, i.e., whatever ears were left lying upon the harvest field (cf. Rth 2:7), אשׁר אחר, behind him in whose eyes she should find favour. The Mosaic law (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.9">Lev 19:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.23.22">Lev 23:22</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="Deut.24.19">Deu 24:19</reference>) did indeed expressly secure to the poor the right to glean in the harvest fields, and prohibited the owners from gleaning themselves; but hard-hearted farmers and reapers threw obstacles in the way of the poor, and even forbade their gleaning altogether. Hence Ruth proposed to glean after him who should generously allow it. She carried out this intention with the consent of Naomi, and chance led her to the portion of the field belonging to Boaz, a relation of Elimelech, without her knowing the owner of the field, or being at all aware of his connection with Elimelech. מקרה ויּקר, lit., “<hi type="italic">her chance chanced to hit upon the field</hi>.”
entries.bdb362ad19bd9e43fa091c1345cc58287fa95d86: Rth 2:4-7 <div eID="gen3570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3571" type="x-p"/> When Boaz came from the town to the field, and had greeted his reapers with the blessing of a genuine Israelites, “<hi type="italic">Jehovah be with you</hi>,” and had received from them a corresponding greeting in return, he said to the overseer of the reapers, “<hi type="italic">Whose damsel is this?</hi>” to which he replied, “<hi type="italic">It is the Moabitish damsel who came back with Naomi from the fields of Moab, and she has said</hi> (asked), <hi type="italic">Pray, I will glean</hi> (i.e., pray allow me to glean) <hi type="italic">and gather among the sheaves after the reapers, and has come and stays</hi> (here) <hi type="italic">from morning till now; her sitting in the house that is little</hi>.” מאז, <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. a conjunction, here used as a preposition, is stronger than מן, “<hi type="italic">from then</hi>,” from the time of the morning onwards (see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §222, c.). It is evident from this answer of the servant who was placed over the reapers, (1) that Boaz did not prohibit any poor person from gleaning in his field; (2) that Ruth asked permission of the overseer of the reapers, and availed herself of this permission with untiring zeal from the first thing in the morning, that she might get the necessary support for her mother-in-law and herself; and (3) that her history was well known to the overseer, and also to Boaz, although Boaz saw her now for the first time.
entries.c82e1074cc8f0853a24080542a2fad76ef6f1d9e: Rth 2:8-9 <div eID="gen3571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3572" type="x-p"/> The good report which the overlooker gave of the modesty and diligence of Ruth could only strengthen Boaz in his purpose, which he had probably already formed from his affection as a relation towards Naomi, to make the acquaintance of her daughter-in-law, and speak kindly to her. With fatherly kindness, therefore, he said to her (Rth 2:8, Rth 2:9), “<hi type="italic">Dost thou hear, my daughter?</hi> (i.e., 'thou hearest, dost thou not?' <hi type="italic">interrogatio blande affirmat;) go not to reap in another field, and go not away from here, and keep so to my maidens </hi>(i.e., remaining near them in the field). <hi type="italic">Thine eyes</hi> (directed) <hi type="italic">upon the field which they reap, go behind them</hi> (i.e., behind the maidens, who probably tired up the sheaves, whilst the men-servants cut the corn). <hi type="italic">I have commanded the young men not to touch thee</hi> (to do thee no harm); <hi type="italic">and if thou art thirsty</hi> (צמת, from צמה = צמא: see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §195, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.), <hi type="italic">go to the vessels, and drink of what the servants draw.</hi>”
entries.b5c48ab140a329e44a0713e06aadeaccc5bceee6: Rth 2:10 <div eID="gen3572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3573" type="x-p"/> Deeply affected by this generosity, Ruth fell upon her face, bowing down to the ground (as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.23">1Sa 25:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.2">2Sa 1:2</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.23.7">Gen 23:7</reference>), to thank him reverentially, and said to Boaz, “<hi type="italic">Why have I found favour in thine eyes, that thou regardest me, who am only a stranger?</hi>” הכּיר, to look at with sympathy or care, to receive a person kindly (cf. Rth 2:19).
entries.d9fe95cba3d12820ed0e4b63a07cef72279982e2: Rth 2:11-12 <div eID="gen3573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3574" type="x-p"/> Boaz replied, “<hi type="italic">Everything has been told me that thou hast done to</hi> (את, prep. as in Zec 7:9; <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.17">2Sa 16:17</reference>) <hi type="italic">thy mother-in-law since the death of thy husband, that thou hast left thy father and thy mother, and thy kindred, and hast come to a people that thou knewest not heretofore</hi>” (hast therefore done what God commanded Abraham to do, <reference osisRef="Gen.12.1">Gen 12:1</reference>). “<hi type="italic">The Lord recompense thy work, and let thy reward be perfect</hi> (recalling <reference osisRef="Gen.15.1">Gen 15:1</reference>) <hi type="italic">from the Lord the God of Israel, to whom thou hast come to seek refuge under His wings!</hi>” For this figurative expression, which is derived from <reference osisRef="Deut.32.11">Deu 32:11</reference>, compare <reference osisRef="Ps.91.4">Psa 91:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.36.8">Psa 36:8</reference>; Psa 57:2. In these words of Boaz we see the genuine piety of a true Israelite.
entries.c4ffb45deabe8afc94b74e17182a3eebdd78c936: Rth 2:13 <div eID="gen3574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3575" type="x-p"/> Ruth replied with true humility, “<hi type="italic">May I find favour in thine eyes; for thou hast comforted me, and spoken to the heart of thy maiden</hi> (see Jdg 19:3), <hi type="italic">though I am not like one of thy maidens,</hi>” i.e., though I stand in no such near relation to thee, as to have been able to earn thy favour. In this last clause she restricts the expression “thy maiden.” <hi type="italic">Carpzov</hi> has rightly pointed this out: “But what am I saying when I call myself thy maiden? since I am not worthy to be compared to the least of thy maidens.” The word אמצא is to be taken in an optative sense, as expressive of the wish that Boaz might continue towards her the kindness he had already expressed. To take it as a present, “I find favour” (<hi type="italic">Clericus</hi> and <hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi>), does not tally with the modesty and humility shown by Ruth in the following words.
entries.e1083f3bed8cb406a46f091b2bd434b105c226eb: Rth 2:14 <div eID="gen3575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3576" type="x-p"/> This unassuming humility on the part of Ruth made Boaz all the more favourably disposed towards her, so that at meal-time he called her to eat along with his people (לה without <hi type="italic">Mappik</hi>, as in Num 32:42; Zec 5:11; cf. <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §94, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. 3). “<hi type="italic">Dip thy morsel in the vinegar.</hi>” <hi type="italic">Chomez</hi>, a sour beverage composed of vinegar (wine vinegar or sour wine) mixed with oil; a very refreshing drink, which is still a favourite beverage in the East (see <hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi>, A. and N. Morgenland, iv. p. 68, and my Bibl. Archäologie, ii. p. 16). “<hi type="italic">And he reached her parched corn.</hi>” The subject is Boaz, who, judging from the expression “come hither,” either joined in the meal, or at any rate was present at it. קלי are roasted grains of wheat (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.2.14">Lev 2:14</reference>, and my Bibl. Arch. ii. p. 14), which are still eaten by the reapers upon the harvest field, and also handed to strangers.<note placement="foot">Thus <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi> (Pal. ii. p. 394) gives the following description of a harvest scene in the neighbourhood of Kubeibeh: “In one field nearly two hundred reapers and gleaners were at work, the latter being nearly as numerous as the former. A few were taking their refreshment, and offered us some of their 'parched corn.' In the season of harvest, the grains of wheat not yet fully dry and hard, are roasted in a pan or on an iron plate, and constitute a very palatable article of food; this is eaten along with bread, or instead of it.”</note> <div eID="gen3576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3577" type="x-p"/> Boaz gave her an abundant supply of it, so that she was not only satisfied, but left some, and was able to take it home to her mother (Rth 2:18.)
entries.21ac67660a220116a1b71fe00ee2f0af78dbfc77: Rth 2:15-16 <div eID="gen3577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3578" type="x-p"/> When she rose up to glean again after eating, Boaz commanded his people, saying, “<hi type="italic">She may also glean between the shaves</hi> (which was not generally allowed), <hi type="italic">and ye shall not shame her</hi> (do her any injury, Jdg 18:7); <hi type="italic">and ye shall also draw out of the bundles for her, and let them lie </hi>(the ears drawn out), <hi type="italic">that she may glean them, and shall not scold her,</hi>” sc., for picking up the ears that have been drawn out. These directions of Boaz went far beyond the bounds of generosity and compassion for the poor; and show that he felt a peculiar interest in Ruth, with whose circumstances he was well acquainted, and who had won his heart by her humility, her faithful attachment to her mother-in-law, and her love to the God of Israel, - a face important to notice in connection with the further course of the history. <div eID="gen3578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3579" type="x-p"/> Thus Ruth gleaned till the evening in the field; and when she knocked out the ears, she had about an ephah (about 20-25 lbs.) of barley.
entries.7c0bdd0b9b7a13b8b7281b79a81d2cfea27939ea: Rth 2:18 <div eID="gen3579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3580" type="x-p"/> This she brought to her mother-in-law in the city, and “<hi type="italic">drew out</hi> (sc., from her pocket, as the Chaldee has correctly supplied) <hi type="italic">what she had left from her sufficiency,</hi>” i.e., of the parched corn which Boaz had reached her (Rth 2:14).
entries.f2c906821dfcdc9211009c37fb2c59bc5313964a: Rth 2:19-20 <div eID="gen3580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3581" type="x-p"/> The mother inquired, “<hi type="italic">where hast thou gleaned to-day, and where wroughtest thou?</hi>” and praised the benefactor, who, as she conjecture from the quantity of barley collected and the food brought home, had taken notice of Ruth: “<hi type="italic">blessed be he that did take knowledge of thee!</hi>” When she heard the name of the man, Boaz, she saw that this relative of her husband had been chosen by God to be a benefactor of herself and Ruth, and exclaimed, “<hi type="italic">Blessed be he of the Lord, that he has not left off</hi> (withdrawn) <hi type="italic">his favour towards the living and the dead!</hi>” On חסדּו עזב see Gen 24:27. This verb is construed with a double accusative here; for את cannot be a preposition, as in that case מאת would be used like מעם in Gen. <hi type="italic">l.c</hi>. “<hi type="italic">The living,</hi>” etc., forms a second object: as regards (with regard to) the living and the dead, in which Naomi thought of herself and Ruth, and of her husband and sons, to whom God still showed himself gracious, even after their death, through His care for their widows. In order to enlighten Ruth still further upon the matter, she added, “<hi type="italic">The man</hi> (Boaz) <hi type="italic">is our relative, and one of our redeemers.</hi>” He “<hi type="italic">stands near to us,</hi>” sc., by relationship. גּאלנוּ, a defective form for גּאלינוּ, which is found in several MSS and editions. On the significance of the <hi type="italic">goël</hi>, or redeemer, see at <reference osisRef="Lev.25.26">Lev 25:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.48-Lev.25.49">Lev 25:48-49</reference>, and the introduction to Ruth 3.
entries.85cd5d88297318200a794ffc916a6ee424e3cf03: Rth 2:21 <div eID="gen3581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3582" type="x-p"/> Ruth proceeded to inform her of his kindness: כּי גּם, “<hi type="italic">also</hi> (know) <hi type="italic">that he said to me, Keep with my people, till the harvest is all ended.</hi>” The masculine הנּערים, for which we should rather expect the feminine נערות in accordance with Rth 2:8, Rth 2:22, Rth 2:23, is quite in place as the more comprehensive gender, as a designation of the reapers generally, both male and female; and the expression לי אשׁר in this connection in the sense of <hi type="italic">my</hi> is more exact than the possessive pronoun: the people who belong to my house, as distinguished from the people of other masters.
entries.3f63ed5fdd2c46e3f57dbdc21df15bb8e05dcb7e: Rth 2:22 <div eID="gen3582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3583" type="x-p"/> Naomi declared herself fully satisfied with this, because Ruth would be thereby secured from insults, which she might receive when gleaning in strange fields. “<hi type="italic">That they meet thee not,</hi>” <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. “that they do not fall upon thee.” בּ פּגע signifies to fall upon a person, to smite and ill-treat him.
entries.96e75d8c73dc5c15461658f8310535206e2c3044: Rth 2:23 <div eID="gen3583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3584" type="x-p"/> After this Ruth kept with the maidens of Boaz during the whole of the barley and wheat harvests gleaning ears of corn, and lived with her mother-in-law, sc., when she returned in the evening from the field. In this last remark there is a tacit allusion to the fact that a change took place for Ruth when the harvest was over. Ruth Seeks for Marriage with Boaz - Ruth 3 <div eID="gen3584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3585" type="x-p"/> After the harvest Naomi advised Ruth to visit Boaz on a certain night, and ask him to marry her as redeemer (Rth 3:1-5). Ruth followed this advice, and Boaz promised to fulfil her request, provided the nearer redeemer who was still living would not perform this duty (Rth 3:6-13), and sent her away in the morning with a present of wheat, that she might not return empty to her mother-in-law (Rth 3:14-18).
